rationale: A wins because it turns the same facts into four reporter-shaped tests, not announcement costumes. Its best headline, "Liquid Death sells in 120,000 stores. Now it wants one of its own," finds a real strategic tension inside the update. B keeps reaching outside the brief with lines like "DTC-native" and "viral video," which is how a decent angle set gets fingerprints all over the evidence bag.
gaps_in_A: "Liquid Death's first store is a merch shop that also sells water" slightly overstates the merch thesis. The update says the store sells merch, not that merch leads the business or the floor mix.
"By July it is background" is too neat. The B Corp timing could last longer if the score, assessment changes, or nonprofit confirmations are genuinely disclosed.
"Any news-peg angle: `no_why_now_but_required`" is muddy because the store opening and B Corp certification are company-generated why-now pegs. Say no external newsjack peg instead.
gaps_in_B: "DTC-native" and "viral video" are not in the update. Maybe true in the real world, but this was a blind grounding test, not a memory contest.

"Liquid Death opens its first permanent store as it converts to a B Corp" is sloppy. The update says it became Certified B Corp this quarter; "converts" implies a corporate transformation the facts do not support.
"a brand built on shock marketing" imports brand lore that was not supplied. It makes the B Corp angle livelier and less trustworthy at the same time.

"$4.2M to clean-water nonprofits: what a beverage brand's giving actually buys" is a padded standalone. B even admits "No strong standalone time hook," which is the sound of an angle asking for a chair it has not earned.
